title: The poem, its title and translator
short: Baudelaire's sonnet 'Correspondances', Les Fleurs du mal (1857), no. IV in 'Spleen et Idéal'; Cyril Scott (1909) retitles it 'Echoes'.
body: 'Correspondances' is the fourth poem of Les Fleurs du mal (1857 and 1861 editions), in the opening section 'Spleen et Idéal', and has long been read as a statement of Baudelaire's poetics and a founding text of French Symbolism. The archive's translation is by Cyril Scott (1879-1970), the English composer, whose Baudelaire: The Flowers of Evil appeared in 1909 (London: Elkin Mathews). Scott replaces the doctrinal title 'Correspondences' with 'Echoes', taken from line 5, which shifts the stress from a metaphysical theory to a sensory, musical effect, perhaps natural for a composer.

title: Nature as temple: the doctrine of correspondences
short: Baudelaire's 'La Nature est un temple': the visible world as a sacred text of signs, an idea drawn from Swedenborg's doctrine of correspondences.
body: The Swedish mystic Emanuel Swedenborg (1688-1772) taught that every natural thing corresponds to a spiritual reality, so that the world is a language in which heaven speaks. Baudelaire knew the doctrine through Balzac's Swedenborgian novels (Louis Lambert, Séraphîta) and wider Romantic illuminism, and the opening quatrain applies it: nature is a 'temple' whose living pillars utter confused words. Critics usually distinguish two kinds of correspondence in the sonnet: 'vertical', between the material and the spiritual worlds (quatrain 1), and 'horizontal', among the senses themselves (from line 8). Scott's 'In Nature's temple' gently converts Baudelaire's statement ('Nature is a temple') into a setting.

title: living columns
short: Baudelaire's 'vivants piliers': trees as the pillars of a forest-temple, the old figure of the forest as cathedral.
body: The image fuses a forest with a temple: tree trunks become pillars, the canopy a vault. The comparison of Gothic churches to forests was famous in French Romanticism through Chateaubriand's Génie du christianisme (1802), which argued that Gothic architecture imitated the forests of the Gauls. Baudelaire reverses the direction: nature itself is the sacred building. 'Vivants' (living) makes the pillars animate, preparing for the 'confused words' they let fall and the 'eyes' of line 4. Scott's 'rise' adds an upward movement not in the French ('où de vivants piliers / Laissent parfois sortir de confuses paroles').

title: words subdued
short: Baudelaire's 'confuses paroles', confused or indistinct words: nature speaks, but not clearly; Scott's 'subdued' makes them quiet rather than obscure.
body: The pillars 'sometimes let out confused words'. The French adjective 'confuses' means indistinct, mingled, hard to make out, and it prepares for 'se confondent' (blend, merge) in line 5: nature's language is a blending, and its meaning is not plain. Scott's 'subdued' suggests low volume rather than mixed or obscure sense, and 'give tongue', an idiom also used of hounds baying, is more vigorous than Baudelaire's 'laissent sortir' (let out). The point for students is that Baudelaire's nature is a text that must be deciphered, which is why the poem was later read as a manifesto of Symbolism.

title: symbolic wood
short: Baudelaire's 'des forêts de symboles', forests of symbols; the famous phrase that the Symbolists took as their watchword.
body: Man passes 'à travers des forêts de symboles', through forests of symbols, which watch him 'avec des regards familiers'. The forest is the temple of line 1 seen from within, and the phrase implies that everything in it signifies something beyond itself. It became a key phrase for the generation of Mallarmé, Verlaine and Rimbaud, and Jean Moréas's 'Symbolist manifesto' (1886) named the movement in Baudelaire's wake. Scott's singular 'symbolic wood' is compact but loses the overwhelming plural of 'forêts'.

title: half familiar eyes
short: Baudelaire's 'regards familiers', familiar looks or gazes: the forest watches man as if it knows him; Scott adds 'half', making the look uncanny.
body: In Baudelaire the symbols observe man 'avec des regards familiers', with familiar glances, a reversal in which nature looks at man rather than the reverse. 'Familier' suggests a knowledge already shared, as if man had once belonged to this world and forgotten it, a Platonic idea of recognition. Scott's 'half familiar' introduces a note of uncanny half-recognition, perhaps reasonable as interpretation but not in the text. 'Regards' (gazes) is plural and active, whereas 'eyes' are organs; the French insists on the act of looking.

title: Like lingering echoes
greek: de longs échos qui de loin se confondent
short: Baudelaire's 'Comme de longs échos qui de loin se confondent': long echoes that merge from a distance, the simile for sensory correspondences.
body: The second quatrain is a single simile: as long echoes from afar blend 'in a dark and deep unity', so scents, colours and sounds answer each other. The echo is apt: it is a sound reflected and returned, so it already embodies 'response', and long echoes heard from far away lose their separate outlines and merge. Scott's 'lingering' renders 'longs' (long, drawn out) well, and his phrase 'afar confound / Themselves' keeps the reflexive verb 'se confondent', though 'confound' in English now usually means bewilder rather than blend. This line gave Scott his title.

title: deep and sombre unity
short: Baudelaire's 'Dans une ténébreuse et profonde unité': the senses merge in a unity that is dark and deep, mystical rather than rational.
body: 'Ténébreuse' (shadowy, obscure) links the unity to night, and the next line compares it to 'la nuit' and 'la clarté': it is as vast as both darkness and light, embracing opposites. The idea of an underlying unity behind diverse sensations is Romantic and mystical; it implies that sensory experience, rightly attended to, gives access to a hidden order. Scott reverses the adjectives ('deep and sombre' for 'ténébreuse et profonde'), which is harmless, but 'sombre' is gloomier than 'ténébreuse', which means not sad but dark and mysterious.

title: transplendency
greek: Latin trans + splendere; French la clarté
short: Scott's rare Latinate word for Baudelaire's 'la clarté' (light, brightness); it means surpassing splendour or radiance.
body: Baudelaire's line is simple: 'Vaste comme la nuit et comme la clarté', vast as night and as light. Scott chooses the unusual 'transplendency', built from Latin trans- (beyond, through) and splendere (to shine), as in the rare adjective 'transplendent', 'shining through or beyond'. The word heightens what in French is a plain noun, a habit typical of Scott's ornate 1909 manner. It also blurs the balance of Baudelaire's line, where night and daylight stand side by side as equal, opposite immensities.

title: The scents and colours to each other respond
greek: Les parfums, les couleurs et les sons se répondent
short: Baudelaire's key line, 'Les parfums, les couleurs et les sons se répondent', names three senses; Scott omits 'les sons', the sounds.
body: Line 8 states the principle of synaesthetic correspondence: perfumes, colours and sounds answer one another. Scott's version drops 'sounds', presumably to fit the line, which is a significant loss in a poem whose next tercet compares scents to oboes. Baudelaire had already put the idea in prose in his Salon de 1846, quoting a passage from E. T. A. Hoffmann's Kreisleriana about the analogy between colours, sounds and scents. In 'Richard Wagner et Tannhäuser à Paris' (1861) he quoted the two quatrains of this sonnet to describe the effect of Wagner's music. Critics debate whether 'Correspondances' describes literal synaesthesia or a poetic doctrine of analogy; the poem supports both readings.

title: like infant's flesh as chaste
short: Baudelaire's 'Il est des parfums frais comme des chairs d'enfants': fresh scents compared to children's skin, smell rendered by touch.
body: The first tercet gives examples of correspondence across the senses: a scent is fresh like children's skin (touch), sweet like oboes (sound), green like meadows (sight). Baudelaire's adjective is 'frais' (fresh, cool); Scott's 'chaste' gives the scent a moral quality and rhymes with 'vast' in line 11, but it shifts the analogy from sensation to virtue. 'Chairs' (flesh) is bodily and unsentimental; the innocence of these scents is physical. The tercet opposes these innocent scents to the 'corrupted' ones of the next lines.

title: As sweet as oboes
greek: Doux comme les hautbois, verts comme les prairies
short: Baudelaire's 'Doux comme les hautbois, verts comme les prairies': scent compared to the sound of oboes and the colour of meadows.
body: This line performs the correspondence that Scott's line 8 partly omitted: a scent is sweet (soft) as the oboe's tone and green as the meadows. 'Hautbois' (literally 'high wood') is the oboe, an instrument associated in French with pastoral music; Baudelaire's chain therefore moves from the oboe's pastoral sound to the green fields. Scott's 'meadows fair' replaces Baudelaire's colour, 'verts' (green), with a general aesthetic adjective, so the visual sense also vanishes; what remains is mainly scent and sound.

title: corrupted ... rich
short: Baudelaire's '— Et d'autres, corrompus, riches et triomphants': opposed to the innocent scents are decadent, luxurious ones; Scott replaces 'triomphants' with 'proud ... vast'.
body: The sonnet turns from fresh, innocent scents to 'others, corrupt, rich and triumphant'. The dash in the French marks the shift. This second class is characteristic of Baudelaire, for whom corruption and splendour are often bound together, as the title Les Fleurs du mal suggests. Many readers think the sonnet's sympathy lies with these heavy, intoxicating scents, since they are given the final, expansive tercet. Scott adds 'proud' and moves 'vast' (for 'triomphants') to the rhyme. 'Corrupted' keeps the moral charge of 'corrompus', which can mean both decayed and morally depraved.

anchor: Which have the expansion of infinity
title: the expansion of infinity
short: Baudelaire's 'Ayant l'expansion des choses infinies': scents that spread out like infinite things, so that a sensation becomes a way to the infinite.
body: The last tercet gives these rich scents a metaphysical scope: they have 'the expansion of infinite things'. 'Expansion' describes the physical spreading of a scent through a room and also an expansion of the soul, so the line moves from physics to spirit, a movement that answers the 'vertical' correspondence of the first quatrain. Scott translates closely, though 'infinity' turns Baudelaire's plural 'choses infinies' (infinite things) into an abstraction. Commentators link this to Baudelaire's essays on intoxication, Les Paradis artificiels (1860), where perfume and drugs expand perception.

anchor: amber, musk and frankincense and myrrh
title: amber, musk and frankincense and myrrh
greek: l'ambre, le musc, le benjoin et l'encens
short: Baudelaire lists 'l'ambre, le musc, le benjoin et l'encens'; Scott substitutes biblical myrrh for benzoin, recalling the gifts of the Magi.
body: Ambergris (ambre), musk, benzoin and incense are animal and resin scents used in perfume and in worship; together they join the erotic boudoir to the church, a typically Baudelairean mixture. Scott keeps 'amber' and 'musk' and renders 'encens' as 'frankincense', but replaces 'benjoin' (benzoin, a balsamic resin from Southeast Asian trees) with 'myrrh', perhaps for metre. 'Frankincense and myrrh' inevitably recalls the gifts of the Magi in Matthew 2:11, so Scott makes the line more biblical and sacred than Baudelaire's, which balances sensual and liturgical scents.

title: the soul's and senses' ecstasy
greek: les transports de l'esprit et des sens; Greek ekstasis
short: Baudelaire's 'Qui chantent les transports de l'esprit et des sens': the scents sing the raptures of mind and senses together.
body: The sonnet ends by joining 'esprit' (mind, spirit) and 'sens' (senses) in one rapture, so that the 'vertical' correspondence of the opening (between the material and the spiritual) and the 'horizontal' correspondence among the senses are reunited. 'Chantent' (sing) brings sound back into a tercet about smell, completing the synaesthesia. 'Transports' means rapture, being carried out of oneself. Scott's 'ecstasy' (from Greek ekstasis, standing outside oneself) is an apt equivalent; the order 'soul's and senses'' keeps the French pairing.

title: Sonnet form
short: A sonnet in alexandrines, rhymed abba abba cdc dee; Scott writes loose pentameters with his own rhymes.
body: Baudelaire's sonnet uses twelve-syllable alexandrines. Its quatrains rhyme abba abba (piliers/paroles/symboles/familiers; confondent/unité/clarté/répondent), with the sestet rhyming cdc dee (enfants/prairies/triomphants; infinies/encens/sens). Scott keeps the octave-sestet division, with the sestet printed as two tercets, but writes ten- or eleven-syllable lines, rhymes the quatrains abba cddc with his own sounds ('confound/respond' is a loose rhyme), and arranges the tercets as efe gfg. The sonnet's traditional turn after line 8 here marks a move from statement of principle (octave) to examples (sestet).

title: Influence
short: 'Correspondances' became a founding text of Symbolism; Rimbaud's 'Voyelles' (vowels as colours) is its most famous successor.
body: Later French poets read the sonnet as a programme: the world as a forest of symbols to be deciphered, and the senses as interchangeable languages. Rimbaud's sonnet 'Voyelles' (c. 1871), assigning colours to vowels, pushes horizontal correspondence to provocation; Mallarmé's poetics of suggestion, and the Symbolist movement named in 1886, are also indebted to it. In English, Arthur Symons's The Symbolist Movement in Literature (1899) helped bring these ideas to Yeats and later modernists. Scott's 1909 translation belongs to that period of English enthusiasm for the French Symbolists.
